utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours have probably notice that had Mr. Zaric is not here with us this morning. I spoke with him yesterday, and also this morning, and he has a scheduled medical examination in the Detention Unit. But he authorised me to inform the Trial Chamber that he waives his right of being here today, so we can go on with proceedings without any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But he also asked me to address the Trial Chamber in respect to his health condition, because he's suffering pains for a couple of months now, and he's on painkillers for days, and hopefully he will have a proper medical examination today. And I will keep the Trial Chamber informed about his health condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We'll go ahead with our witness. Can the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pistoljevic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to put questions to you, but I would kindly ask you to wait a few seconds after I've finished my questions so that it can be translated, and then give me your answer. And I will also wait for you to finish your answer, in order to avoid overlapping our questions and answers. Will you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Mustafa Pistoljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's Dzigara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and where were you born, Mr. Pistoljevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac, on the 24th of October, 1934.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I am a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are your ancestors also from the area of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean my family?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, your fathers, your grandfathers, your ancestors.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us: What ethnicity is your wife?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: She is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I have two daughters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of school did you finish? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Four years of elementary school and two years of vocational school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, tell us: Just where did you work? In which company did you work?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I worked in Bosanski Samac, Mebos, Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber: When were you retired?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you complete military service, or can you remember when was that, and did you finish it with a rank?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I went to the army in 1954, and I have the rank of a private first class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us also, Mr. Pistoljevic: Were you or are you now a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: When the communists were there, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and after its disintegration you were not a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after we have recorded your details, now, Mr. Pistoljevic, I will question you briefly about the events in Samac that took place in 1992, and then I'll ask you about the thing that I'm most interested in, and that is your exchange. Have you ever heard of the 4th Detachment or -- and were you a member of this 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I've heard about it, but I wasn't in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me: Did you know Mr. Miroslav Tadic before the war, and what was your relationship with him? Was he just an acquaintance of yours or were you close?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know him. We grew up together in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you socialising with him extensively before the war or did you just know him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew him, but we didn't socialise, because he had his team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, just briefly: After the events in April 1992, more precisely, the 16th and 17th of April, did you work at the local Red Cross organisation, and can you briefly describe what was your role?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out, we distributed milk and bread, and I did it from my home. They gave me this job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps when were you arrested? First of all, let me ask you: Were you arrested in 1992? And then, if you were, tell me when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: That was in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Pistoljevic: Do you have a brother, and what is his name?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. His name is Hasan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he also arrested at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: He was arrested later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Chamber: Who arrested you? Was it the police? Did you report yourself, or did anyone come to pick you up?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The police came with a car, and they drove me away, and then some fortnight later, my brother was taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know: Did the police search your flat?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what was the reason for your arrest? Were you told that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were stories going around that allegedly we had weapons, but we didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten at the police station, Mr. Pistoljevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone beat you at the police station after you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly: When did that take place, and who beat you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: His name was Boban Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: He was a police officer in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he beat you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: He had a plastic sabre, and he hit me on the head, on the back, also on the arms, because I tried to protect myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten several times or only once, now that you have described it? Did anyone else beat you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that man beat you several times?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you remained at the police station, and were you transferred someplace else?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was at the police station for 21 days, and then we were transferred to the TO, which is just across the street from SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the TO, were you taken for questioning by inspectors? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I've already forgotten, but once he came and asked us why we were imprisoned, and when I read what I stated, I signed that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. For the sake of clarity: On page 6, lines 21 and following, you asked whether the witness was taken for questioning by inspectors and the answer on line 23 was, the witness says: "He came and asked us why we were there," et cetera. I think we should have some clarity who the "he" was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was exactly what I intended to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of that man who came and asked you, or questioned you, and then gave you statements to sign?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. People were coming and going in the SUP while we were imprisoned there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will try to refresh your memory. You just tell me if that man's name was Inspector Simo Bozic, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Simo Bozic questioned me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when you were transferred to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: We were transferred to Batkovic, a group of people was transferred by bus to Batkovic. It was on the 28th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the same year?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of that same year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your brother transferred with you to Batkovic as well?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He spent a short time at the SUP, and we saw each other, and they couldn't put us together there. He wasn't beaten at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, tell us: Did you see Miroslav Tadic in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I saw him when he came, when we were about to go home. I asked a man there, because I couldn't see very well - I had an eye surgery, and the bulb up there was very small - and he came and called out our names --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you wait? Wait a second, please. Did he tell you why he was calling up your names? Was it for exchange? Was there any mention of the reason for calling up your names?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't call up my name, but rather, I asked another detainee: Could you please look -- is there my name on the list? Do you see the name of Mustafa Pistoljevic? Then Tadic turned around, before I finished, and he told me: You are going home. These were his exact words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since Tadic told you that, did they continue to call up the names?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. There was a big bus there, because the majority of people were there were Serbs, a few Croats --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please wait a second, Mr. Pistoljevic. We are talking about the departure from Batkovic. Later we'll discuss the return. Now, when you boarded the bus in Batkovic, what was the ethnicity of the people who boarded the bus in Batkovic when you set off from Batkovic? What was the ethnicity of those people? Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know them. There were a few people from Samac, maybe four or five of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: While you were on the bus and you set off from Batkovic, did you discuss anything with Tadic? Did you ask him about an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked him, when we set off -- in fact, he told me, by himself: Mustafa, you are free to go, or even if you want to proceed to Croatia, and also you can return to your home. I said: I'm not going anywhere from my house, because that's the best place for me to live. And when we arrived in Dragalic across the River Sava, Bosanska Gradiska, I was told: Here is an opportunities for you. If you don't feel like going home, there is a man from Croatia. And he asked me: Would I like to stay there? But I said: No. I'm going back home. Because I was told, while on the bus, that it was possible for me to go home, and I wished to do so, because I left my house there and I was thinking why I shouldn't go back there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us: Did anyone tell you that if you didn't want to go to Croatia you had to go back to the prison in Batkovic, or rather, did they tell you that if you didn't want to go to Croatia you were free to go home?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no one said any such thing. I didn't hear anyone say anything like that. People were talking when we were on our way to Vojnic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hold on a second, please. We'll proceed with that now. When you arrived in Dragalic, who exactly did you tell that you didn't want to cross to the other side, namely, to Croatia? Who asked you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Miro. I think that was the man's name. Miro Tadic. He said: You, if you want to go to Croatia now, or anywhere else, this man here will help you; if not, you're free to go back to your home in Samac. And then I confirmed yet again that I wanted to go straight home, and that was the only place I wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember: In addition to yourself, were there other people who made the same decision as you, namely, to go home?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: There was a Muslim and a Croat. The two of them were from Bosanski Samac and they went back home from Dragalic. I think that was the name of the village. The two of them went back. And those Serbs who came, the exchange, you know, Muslims and Croats --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember: When you went to Dragalic by bus from Batkovic, did you go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreters didn't get the last part of the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that those people came back with you. Can you just repeat the last sentence, because the line was bad. The Serbs who came back, as well as Muslims and Croats who came back, who were the Croats and Muslims who came back with you from Dragalic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I only know about the two who came with me and who sat with me. I only knew about those two. But they are somewhere abroad now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall: On your way from Batkovic to Dragalic, when you left the prison, did the bus pass through Samac, and did other people join the bus in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many additional people boarded the bus in Samac? Just approximately, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: One of them was ill. He was on dialysis. That man sat with me and he left for Holland eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mustafa, do you know a man named Veljo Maslic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: They asked me about him. I remember as if through a mist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No problem if you don't recall. What happened on the way back from Dragalic, when you headed towards Samac? Did you stop anywhere? What happened there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Once we crossed the River Sava and came to Bosanska Gradiska, there was a Serbian church there, and it was Christmastime. They invited us to go there to have dinner there, to sit down and get some rest. We all went there. No one stayed in the bus. We stayed there for about half an hour, perhaps three quarters of an hour. We rested there. We had some food. It was quite a treat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mustafa: Did you immediately go in to eat or only after someone had invited you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A man came, and we hadn't yet started out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "we"? Who hadn't yet started?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The other two men who were with me, I told them: You needn't talk now. I'll do the talking for you. Because we were together there on our way back, so I told them not to talk, that I would do the talking for them. And a Serb man came along and asked me: Mustafa, why aren't you coming? And then he said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Why aren't you coming where?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: He meant over there, to sit down, relax, get some food. I said: We are a minority. That's why we're not coming. And then he called out Miro Tadic's name: Miro, come over. And then Miro came back immediately. He said: Miro, take a look. Here's Dzigara and those other two men. They don't want to go over there and have dinner. And he said: Well, why don't you go? Come on, Mustafa. There's no problem. All three of you. Just you go. Get a proper meal. And then we did go eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you reached Samac, did you go straight home or did you first go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I went to see my son-in-law and my daughter. I asked the bus driver to take me as far as Zlatko's flat. Zlatko is my son-in-law. There was a curfew and this was 2.00 in the morning, perhaps 3.00 in morning. That's when I came, and I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Court: Your son-in-law, what's his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: He's a Croat. Zlatko Stanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he too had been detained in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was detained in Batkovic, and he was in Samac. I still don't know for how long, but he had not been detained for a very long time. He's a very able mechanic. He went to the fields. He carried out repairs, electricity repairs, so they could go on working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, tell us, please: Go on. Once he was released from detention, did he stay in Samac to live there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please: At that time, did you have any family that was elsewhere in Orasje, not in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They had sent a message to me, but the message never reached me, that my relatives had been looking for me. As my mother --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they looking for you, or what did they want? Did they want you to go to Orasje?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They wanted me to go to Orasje, because my mother had been born in Orasje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your brother, Hasan? Tell us in a few words, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Hasan stayed in Samac after his release from prison, and he was there until recently. We are both retirees since 1991, in my case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your brother tell you that he also went for an exchange, only to tell the other side that he did not wish to be exchanged, once they had left Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't go together then. He stayed back in Batkovic and I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do know that, but afterwards, when he left Batkovic, did you also go to the separation line, only to tell the other side that he did not wish to go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I never asked him, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that night, where did you go the next day after you returned to Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I stayed with my son-in-law for the whole of that day. He wasn't working, because the company had ceased to operate. I stayed there with them, with my son-in-law and my daughter, for two days. And then I simply went home to see what was left of it. And then they told me to come back for lunch or dinner. That's exactly what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone in your flat, or was the flat empty once you got there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. It wasn't empty. Nothing was missing. My daughter remained with her husband, Zlatko, and her children. She remained in Samac. She did some gardening. She would go back to her own flat in the evening. So nothing was missing, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court: Where was your wife at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: She was in Zasavica. Zasavica. The distance between Zasavica and Samac is about 7 kilometres. In -- let me think - June, July, the police took her to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please also tell me: How long did she stay in Zasavica for? Did you go about asking for her release?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to that man, to Stiv, in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Stevan Todorovic, chief of police asked a police officer: Who should I speak to about my wife? So they let her go. And they said: Well, there's no one else to talk to aside from Stiv.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened once you went to see Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: He said that the circumstances were still not right for them to let her go. I knew what he was like, so I didn't repeat my request. I just said thank you and I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was your wife finally released? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: In June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year? The same year that you were released from Batkovic? Was it the same year?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I came home on the 7th of January. I was released. June or thereabouts, that was when she came back. Some police officers brought her home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the same year?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: 1991. I'm a bit confused. The same --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Did she return home six months after you did?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay at your flat this whole time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother and his family --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you still reside in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Mr. Pistoljevic: When you talked to Tadic in the bus, when he told you that you were free to go home, did you believe him that you would indeed be released and go home if he told you so?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said: Well, I have nowhere else left to go but my home. He said this twice, possibly even three times, as we were in the bus travelling towards Croatia. He said this several times. He said: You're free to go, but you can go somewhere else too, should you choose to go somewhere else. You may perhaps want to go to Croatia, if you don't want to return to Samac, to your home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. This completes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Cross-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: I take it there's no Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. They would have indicated, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, if Your Honours please. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, what were you arrested for?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Allegedly, my brother and I had been in possession of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, like I said, what I told you before is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no basis for these -- for the arrest?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This was after you had spent time working for the Red Cross distributing milk?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You got the job distributing milk very soon after the 16th and 17th of April, didn't you, around the 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I was distributing milk, milk and bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: They came to my house and told me to go on distributing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But you did that as part of your work at the Red Cross, and you started doing that work at the Red Cross very soon after the 16th and 17th of April, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start doing the work for the Red Cross distributing milk?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, right at the beginning, at the beginning, as soon as the whole mess started. They came to me and they said: You can distribute milk and bread. I kept doing it for perhaps about ten days, and then I said: Well, will you please replace me? I can't go on doing this. And then they sent a younger person over to continue my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it Mr. Tadic who got you the job distributing milk in the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see him at all. He never even passed by just to check. I've never seen him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, let's just turn to the circumstances of your arrest. If you can possibly answer questions with a yes or a no, that will speed up things. You were kept in the SUP for a short period of time and then taken over to the TO. Altogether, how long were you in the SUP and the TO?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-one days I spent at the SUP, and then they transferred me immediately to the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long in the TO?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Twenty -- let me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately. I don't need a precise date, time.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I have April on my mind. Are you asking me about the milk?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think to assist the witness, you simply ask him: When did he leave the TO. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave the TO?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were in the SUP building and in the TO building, of what ethnicity were your fellow prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them being beaten and tortured on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we weren't able to see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to hear men being tortured and beaten on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did hear some noise and commotion coming from a distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, isn't it the truth of the matter that in the SUP building and the TO building, beatings, torture, pulling of teeth, the use of clubs and other instruments, was a daily feature for you and the other prisoners who were held in the TO and the SUP?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that it wasn't. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the only reason that those prisoners were in there, as far as you can tell, was because they were Muslim and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the only time anyone ever asked you or spoke to you about the reason you were in there was the police inspector, and he had to ask you why you were there, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was Simo Bozic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But he didn't know why you were there. He had to ask you, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I did tell him something, but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, after you were transferred -- sorry. Let me rephrase that. You were transferred in November from the TO building to Batkovic. Were you told why you were being taken to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: We all found out why it was, because one detainee got killed, a prisoner. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the prisoner killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: A shell fell into the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever informed or told that you were a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what they told us in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that apply to all of the people in Batkovic, as far as you were aware, that is, all the prisoners in Batkovic were supposedly prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: There were many of us there in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Pistoljevic. I understand that there were many of you there. But can you tell us if you were informed or if you found out or if you knew that you and the other men --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Whether I was a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us if you were informed that the other men who were imprisoned with you were also supposed to be prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, whether I was a prisoner of war. They came to ask us, and they didn't give us anything, and I don't know what they wrote on paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, let's start again and quickly go through this. It won't take long. I'm sure we can get to the bottom of it. First of all, let's start with you. When you were in Batkovic, were you told or informed that you were a prisoner of war? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what you were there for?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I have just told you: A man was killed on the compound of the TO in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as far as the other prisoners of war are concerned, that is, not you, but the other men who were imprisoned there, were you told that they were prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Truly, Mr. Pistoljevic, I make an objection, because I don't think this witness is qualified to say whether anyone was a prisoner of war or not. Maybe we could ask him what his notion of a prisoner of war is. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not seeking a legal conclusion from this man. That's not my purpose at all. It's just if he was given information, told by someone, A, if he was -- as to his status or as to the other status. I'm not asking for his legal conclusions as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The question is proper, because he's just asking whether the witness was told. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Pistoljevic, just can you tell us: Were you informed that the other men who were in prison with you in Batkovic were prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you about this. While we were discussing it among ourselves, one would say we were POWs, the other would say we were this and that. But we didn't arrive at any conclusion of whether we were or we weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So the clear, certain thing is that no one ever told you that you were a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to the occasion when you made your way out of Batkovic. You say that Mr. Tadic came on that day and he informed -- or he had a list on which there were a number of men, you included?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my name was on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic himself speak to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you how it happened. He stood behind -- in front of me, and I asked another detainee who was there with me in my company, and I asked him: Please, will you take a look and see if there's a Pistoljevic name on the list, and at that moment Tadic turned around and told me that I was on the list, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you made any moves to place yourself on that list?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I just asked whether my name was there, and he said: Yes, there was. And that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say, wouldn't it, that you and the other prisoners who were there were desperate to get out of Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, of course we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men were clamouring and gathering around Mr. Tadic, waiting to see if their name was on the list and if they could leave?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were men around him. They gathered there. He called names and they went out. But I don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Batkovic, was it the army who guarded you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, there were, but not all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else, apart from the army, guarded you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Just the army. There was no one else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to be clear about it. The people who were holding you in custody, guarding you and the other prisoners, that was the army, wasn't it? It was the army throughout the period of time that you were in Batkovic, members of the army of the Republika Srpska? Has my answer been -- Mr. Pistoljevic, did you hear my last question? I'll repeat it if you wish. Is it necessary? Did you hear my --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think you had better -- he didn't hear you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Pistoljevic. I'll repeat my question. I want to be clear. The people who were holding you in custody and guarding you and the other prisoners, that was the army, the army of the Republika Srpska, throughout the period of time that you were at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the army. Yes, yes, it was the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the actual transport from Batkovic, on the way from Batkovic to Bosanski Samac, did the bus stop at any military posts?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: It was -- the snow was very big at the time. Yes, we stopped, because we had a punctured tyre. Two tyres were punctured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not asking about mechanical problems that you had, but this: As far as you could see, did the bus stop at any military outposts or any military posts, and did Mr. Tadic conduct any sort of negotiation or speak to army people?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: While I was watching him, he was all the time in the bus, and we travelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd like to show the witness a document, if Your Honours please. It's a document that was provided to us by the Defence. There are sufficient copies, and I'd like it to be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, I'll show you a document that I think relates to your exchange, and just wait a moment while it's prepared on the machine so that you can see it. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I have extra copies for the Bench which can be provided to you. If Your Honours please, I have a draft translation of this particular document, and the full translation will be made available very soon, in a matter of days. So I'd ask that -- eventually I'll be asking for it to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Di Fazio, was not -- a copy wasn't given to the registry assistant so that it can be given to the witness there? MR. DI FAZIO: No. No. I've only just found this document in the last few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, we'll see whether he'll be able to read on the screen. MR. DI FAZIO: I appreciate that, if Your Honours please. It may be difficult. I don't know how --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see anything here. MR. DI FAZIO: May I ask the usher if the machine is functioning at this stage?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, can you see this document at all?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't see my name here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But just tell me this: Can you see -- can you see the writing? Just tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay. There I am. There I am. Yes. But my name wasn't here, on this piece of paper. My name wasn't this high up on the list. My name was lower down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Okay. Fine. Just slow down, and I'll ask you the questions. I'll ask you the questions about it. First of all, under number 5, that is you, isn't it? You were born in 1934?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: But this is not how my name was written. It was lower down on the list, way down the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly, Mr. Pistoljevic. I'm not taking issue with you on that. But let's forget about the document that you saw in prison in Batkovic and let's just concentrate on this particular document, okay? Further down, at the bottom of the document, Mr. Pistoljevic, you'll see the words "above persons handed over," and there's a name under that, Corporal Osapovic, Milorad --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Belgrade] May I please ask that the document be moved up or down so that he can see. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it's after the number 30. MR. DI FAZIO: That's right. At the bottom of the document -- Ms. Usher, can you shift the document so that we can see.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Belgrade] Last name [inaudible]. That's fine. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the bottom of the document now, Mr. Pistoljevic, the signatures at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the signatures. But I can't see my name anywhere. There is the year there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pistoljevic, if you'd just let me finish a question, we can get through this really quickly, and I'll focus your attention on what I want, okay? At the bottom of the document --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the document, it says that a Corporal Milorad Osapovic handed the above persons over and they were taken over by Mr. Miroslav Tadic. And then there's a stamp of the Bijeljina military post, number 7102. Do you see those features? Do you see that at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't. I had an eye surgery. My eyesight is not that good really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you just move this paper, take it away, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I just -- can I just ask you, if you may -- you saw this before. Look at number 5, your name, please, number 5.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You can see that, can you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I can. The year of birth, everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Next to that, to your name, is the words, in handwriting: "He" goes as a civilian." Can you see that? Or rather: "Goes" as civilian." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you this: Did anyone tell you that you were to be exchanged -- did anyone tell you that -- did anyone tell you that you were to be exchanged as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I found it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Pistoljevic, let's return to number 5. Do you see the words: "Goes" as a civilian"? Do you see that in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Belgrade] It's not very legible. What the witness saw earlier was his name, Mustafa. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I've done with the document. And if Your Honours please, can I ask that it be marked for identification? I intend to tender it in due course into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it can be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P168 and ter ID. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Senad Mehmedovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mehmedovic. Yes, I do know him, but I lost track of him about ten years ago, since he was no longer in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he on the exchange with you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Safet Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Safet was there. I do know him. The bus from Bosanski Samac -- we took the bus from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Safet, is he the brother of Izet Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he the chap who had the kidney problems?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. He had kidney problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Andrija Jovic exchanged on the same occasion as you were, and was Marijan Papic also exchanged on the same occasion as you were?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know these people. The bus was quite a big one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bosanski Samac, did you stay the night there before continuing on to Dragalic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: We arrived at about 2.00, past midnight, and we went to the school building. The room was warm. We spent the night there and slept until the next morning. Then we woke up and we again boarded the bus and left for Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see other people being added onto the bus in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: There were many, many people there. The others took their seats, those who were from Batkovic. They boarded the bus, and they wouldn't let any outsiders onto the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean civilians from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Whether they went to those exchanges? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were civilians from Bosanski Samac the ones who were not allowed onto the bus?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: There were some, but they didn't get onto the bus, because there were seats for us to go to Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you and the other men from Batkovic were kept separate and as a group all the way from Batkovic to Bosanski Samac and then again separate and as a group all the way from Bosanski Samac to Dragalic; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: We came to Samac from -- what was it? Batkovic, about 2.00. We sat down, sat ourselves down in that room over there, and then whoever could got some sleep. At about 8.00 or half past 8.00 in the morning we left for Bosanska Gradiska. We had to cross the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Pistoljevic, you've told us that you were never informed as to whether or not you were a prisoner of war while you were in Batkovic. Were you told if you were a prisoner of war at any time during the trip to Dragalic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult to remember that now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Dragalic, that's when Mr. Tadic informed you that you were free to go home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is what he told me: Here, this man, he'll receive you if you want to go to Croatia. But even in Batkovic, I told Tadic that I wanted to go back home. That was where I wanted to go, and not anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of your family was at that stage still in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No one had requested you from Croatia? No one had asked for you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: From Orasje they requested. From Orasje. Both myself and my brother. We have relatives over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to Dragalic: Did you ever speak to any man other than Mr. Tadic about whether or not you wanted to cross over?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I talked to him -- well, he asked me two or three times whether I wanted to go or not. He said: You say you didn't want to go, didn't you? And he said: Yeah, that's one thing you should know. I don't want to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's Mr. Tadic who said that to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only person you spoke to about whether or not you wanted to cross over was Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that may have been someone else, as we were sitting there and talking. Someone else may have said that to me, but Tadic certainly did ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, by asking this last question, the Prosecutor is trying to confuse the witness, because I think the witness said during his examination-in-chief that he also told the other side clearly whether he wanted to go or not. And now, on page 29, line 17, we find something that might indeed confuse the witness. He was quite determined, and when he said that the other side had asked him whether he wanted to go or not, and he said this a number of times, not merely once. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pistoljevic. You've heard what Defence counsel had to say. Is it the case that someone other than Mr. Tadic asked you many times about whether or not you wished to cross?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I think he was sort of pulling my leg also, a little bit, at least, Tadic, I mean. He cracked a few jokes. And then I said: I'm going back home. That's the only place I'm ever going. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Pistoljevic. Did Mr. Tadic, as far as you know, speak to the other two men who also returned to Samac with you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The other two who were there, they didn't even -- they couldn't even speak properly, so I'm quite sure that he didn't talk to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean, they couldn't -- what do you mean, they couldn't even speak properly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, because I told them: Please keep quiet when the three of us go there together. We'll go there together and I'll do the talking. And they agreed. When one of them was not quite sane, so he talked a lot of gibberish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pistoljevic. Now, you -- your wife was in Zasavica. Why was she there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: She is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpretation didn't get the answer. The line was too bad. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, can you just repeat your last answer? You started off by saying: "She is a Croat." What was the rest of your answer?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She is a Croat, and that's why she had been taken away. It was not only her; there were a number of women like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's right, isn't it, Mr. Pistoljevic? Zasavica was full of Croats who had been taken there and isolated, wasn't it, and the same applied to your wife?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you were eventually reunited with her, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I went and I found a police officer who was guarding them. I knew the police officer well, and he knew me. I said: Well, this is what I need. And he said: Well, it's okay for you to go as long as I'm here. So that's how I came there, and I spent some time sitting there with my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you succeed in taking her out of Zasavica and taking her back to live with you in Bosanski Samac, in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I was not able to do that, but I did go to see Stiv.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, can you tell us how long after you saw Stiv Todorovic that you were reunited with your wife?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: How many times did I see him? Is that what you mean? I went there every week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pistoljevic, how long after you saw Todorovic and spoke to him about your wife, how long after that did you succeed in living again with your wife, in getting her to come back and reunite with you and continue your life together? How long after you went to see Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Five and a half or six months later, she was driven in a police car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And did Mr. Tadic have anything to -- was he able to help you reunite with your wife?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I rarely saw Tadic. I seldom saw him. And when I went to Zasavica, I didn't see him even once. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome. Re-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pistoljevic, I will just ask you to clarify one thing: The Prosecutor asked you, when Simo Bozic, inspector, came, and that he asked you why you were arrested, tell us just: Did you hear that anyone had reported you for having weapons? And if you heard such thing, who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I heard it from Milos Sljoko, but that man is deceased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the man who reported you for having weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he has passed away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear from that Milos Sljoko reported you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA PISTOLJEVIC
utterances.text: They are both my neighbours, but they are both deceased. And he told me in Orasje that it was Sljoko who put both himself and myself in prison because of possessing firearms. But they are both dead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pistoljevic, for giving evidence to the Tribunal. We are now finished with you. You may leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We don't have any other witness today. We are continuing with Mr. Savo Popovic on Monday at 0900 hours. We shall rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 11.54 a.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of March 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
